bibliography.abstract: Abstract Residential relocation can disrupt habitual behaviours, offering a window of opportunity for encouraging sustainable lifestyle changes. This study tested the effectiveness of a personalised, web-based intervention aimed at reducing travel- and energy-related emissions among recent movers in Norway (n = 212). The intervention, delivered three months post-relocation, provided tailored feedback on participants’ carbon footprints and interactive behavioural suggestions. Outcomes included weekly car use, overnight car trips, flight frequency, and electricity consumption. Participants who received the intervention made significantly fewer weekly car trips (− 20%), and fewer overnight car trips (− 32%) than the control group. No significant differences were found for flight frequency or electricity consumption. The effect on weekly car use was moderated by changes in dwelling type: Among apartment-to-house movers, the intervention effect was pronounced. Among house-to-apartment movers, effects were smaller and short-lived. Movers to the same dwelling type were unaffected. Contrary to expectations, moving over longer distances did not enhance intervention effects. The findings support the habit discontinuity hypothesis, suggesting that interventions timed with relocation can facilitate behavioural change, particularly when the move is sufficiently disruptive. Directionality also matters: interventions can help maintain low car use among movers to more car-dependent environments. Additionally, the combination of high- and low-impact behavioural suggestions may have influenced participants’ focus, with more salient travel-related changes prioritised over energy-saving actions. These results highlight the importance of tailoring post-move interventions to the type and direction of relocation and carefully framing behavioural options to support broad and lasting change.

en.caveats: The study relies on a relatively small sample size of 212 participants in a single national context, and the observed behavioral changes did not extend to air travel or household electricity use.
en.what: A randomized controlled trial evaluated a personalized, web-based carbon footprint intervention delivered three months post-relocation to 212 recent movers in Norway. The intervention led to a 20% reduction in weekly car trips and a 32% reduction in overnight car trips compared to the control group, though it had no significant effect on flight frequency or electricity consumption. The reduction in weekly car use was strongest among participants who moved from apartments to houses, while those moving from houses to apartments showed smaller, short-lived effects, and those moving between the same dwelling types showed no change.
en.why: The study provides empirical evidence for the habit discontinuity hypothesis, demonstrating that residential relocation creates a window of opportunity where personalized interventions can successfully curb car use. It reveals that the effectiveness of such interventions depends heavily on the direction of the housing transition, showing they can help maintain low-car habits even when people move into more car-dependent housing types.
